t: Cracking the Safe — De Bruijn Sequences via Eulerian Circuits
o:
## Understanding the problem

We need the shortest string such that every possible n-digit password over alphabet {0..k-1} appears as a contiguous substring. There are $k^n$ passwords, and a string of length $k^n + n - 1$ contains exactly that many windows of length n, so if we can make every window distinct, that length is optimal.

**Example 1** (n=1, k=2): each digit is itself a password, so "10" covers both in length 2 = 2^1 + 1 - 1.

**Example 2** (n=2, k=2): "01100" has windows 01, 11, 10, 00 — all four pairs appear once; length 5 = 2^2 + 2 - 1.

Constraints are tiny ($k^n \le 4096$), so even exponential-ish search works, but the elegant solution models this as finding an Eulerian circuit.
k: The answer must have length exactly k^n + n - 1 since a string of that length has k^n windows of size n and we need all of them distinct.
Modeling each (n-1)-digit string as a node and each n-digit string as an edge turns the problem into finding an Eulerian circuit — every edge used exactly once.
A greedy DFS (Hierholzer-style) that always tries digits in order and backtracks when stuck produces a valid de Bruijn sequence.

a.n: Approach 1: Backtracking search for a de Bruijn sequence
a.i: Build the answer greedily: start with n zeros, then repeatedly append any digit whose resulting new n-length suffix hasn't been seen yet. If no digit works, backtrack. Since a de Bruijn sequence always exists, this search succeeds quickly for the tiny constraints.
s: Start the string with n copies of '0' and mark that window visited.
At each step try appending digits 0..k-1; take the first digit making the last-n window unvisited.
Mark it visited and recurse; if stuck, undo and try the next digit.
Stop when the number of visited windows equals k^n; return the accumulated string.
a.t: O(k^(k^n) * n) worst case for the naive bound, but in practice near-linear in output size because greedy choices rarely fail badly; fine for k^n <= 4096.
a.sp: O(k^n * n) to store visited windows and the recursion/path.

a.n: Approach 2: Eulerian circuit on de Bruijn graph (optimal)
a.i: Treat each (n-1)-digit string as a vertex and each n-digit string w as an edge from w's prefix to w's suffix. Every password corresponds to exactly one edge, so we need a trail using all edges: an Eulerian circuit. The graph is balanced (in-degree = out-degree = k at every vertex) and strongly connected, so an Eulerian circuit exists. Hierholzer's algorithm finds one in linear time without backtracking.
s: Start from vertex '0' repeated n-1 times.
DFS: from current vertex v, follow any unused edge v -> (v[1:] + d), marking edges used by tracking visited vertices count or removing edges.
When a vertex has no unused outgoing edges, prepend its label to the answer (post-order).
The final concatenation of vertex labels gives a string of length k^n + n - 1 containing every password exactly once.
a.t: O(k^n * n) — each of the k^n edges is traversed once, with O(n) string slicing per step.
a.sp: O(k^n * n) for the visited-edge set and recursion stack.

w:
## Wrap-up

In an interview, mention the lower-bound argument (length k^n + n - 1) first, then present the Eulerian-circuit model as the key insight; Approach 1 is a good fallback if you can't recall Hierholzer's algorithm. Common pitfalls: forgetting the n=1 case (vertices are empty strings), off-by-one between nodes of length n-1 and edges of length n, and forgetting to append the starting vertex at the end. Follow-ups might ask why the graph is guaranteed Eulerian (balanced degrees plus connectivity) or how to generalize to arbitrary alphabets.
